tldr: Focusing on the difference in timescales between vision and touch, this paper presents a lightweight Flow Matching framework that jointly predicts future world states and generates robot action chunks, achieving high precision in contact-rich tasks alongside an inference latency of just 11.9 ms.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of Agile-WAM. Visual, tactile, and proprioceptive observations are projected once into a shared latent space. A lightweight Flow Matching network then jointly generates action chunks and future visual/tactile latents in a streamlined, non-redundant structure.
overview:
In contact-rich manipulation tasks such as gear meshing or connector insertion, visual information alone cannot capture subtle force adjustments or microscopic misalignments. Integrating tactile feedback into World Action Models (WAMs)—which generate actions while predicting environmental dynamics—has drawn significant attention. However, existing models rely on large-scale pretrained video generation backbones, resulting in heavy computational overhead that makes them unsuitable for high-speed, on-robot real-time control.

The authors focused on the insight that vision and tactile signals evolve at inherently different timescales. Adjacent camera frames change smoothly, so predicting immediate next-step visual states provides little useful supervision. On the other hand, tactile sensor signals spike abruptly upon contact; predicting too far into the future causes the model to miss crucial, fine-grained contact transitions. To address this, the study introduces multi-horizon multimodal prediction: the visual latent is supervised at a larger temporal offset (matching the action chunk execution horizon), while the tactile latent is predicted at the very next frame. In addition, the system adopts a direct vision-tactile-to-action Flow Matching design that maps directly from observation latents to targets, completely eliminating computationally heavy cross-attention.

Evaluated across nine simulated tasks and five challenging real-world contact-rich tasks, Agile-WAM achieved a 29.4% relative gain in overall success rate over baseline methods in physical robot experiments, all while maintaining an inference latency of just 11.9 ms on an RTX 4090. This work clearly demonstrates that an agile, accurate tactile world model can be built from scratch without relying on massive generative backbones, simply by matching the prediction horizons to the physical timescales and leveraging direct generative flows.
contributions: Proposed Agile-WAM, which integrates visual and tactile observations into a shared latent space and directly generates action chunks and future state predictions via lightweight Flow Matching without cross-attention.

Introduced multi-horizon multimodal prediction—supervising slower-moving vision at a longer horizon and rapid-changing tactile signals at the immediate next frame—which dramatically improves learning efficiency for contact dynamics.

Demonstrated superior success rates over state-of-the-art diffusion and flow-based baselines across 9 simulated and 5 real-world contact-rich tasks, while achieving a low inference latency of 11.9 ms on a physical robot.

sections.heading: Why do tactile world models need agility and timescale separation?
sections.summary: While World Action Models achieve strong control performance by jointly predicting future environment states and generating actions, existing tactile-enabled models rely on heavy, pretrained video generation backbones. This paper overcomes this bottleneck by combining multi-horizon prediction tailored to visual and tactile timescales with a lightweight Flow Matching backbone.
sections.details:
When a robot interacts physically with its environment, vision alone quickly hits its limits. In tasks involving rigid contact, two scenarios can look virtually identical visually while experiencing completely different contact forces. Combining visual data with tactile sensing—specifically TacFF (tactile force field) sensors in this study, which capture the magnitude and direction of contact forces—becomes essential.

Recently, researchers have begun incorporating touch into World Action Models (WAMs), which simultaneously model action generation and the forward physical dynamics of the environment. However, many of these approaches build on large pretrained video generation models, consuming massive computational resources during inference. Such heavy models cannot be deployed onboard robots requiring high control frequencies. The central question of this paper is: can we build an agile tactile world model that retains predictive capability while running with minimal latency?

The key insight lies in the different temporal dynamics of vision and touch. Adjacent camera frames are often highly similar; asking the model to predict just one step ahead offers trivial supervision that teaches little meaningful dynamics. Conversely, tactile signals spike abruptly upon contact; predicting several steps into the future causes the model to miss delicate, transient contact dynamics.

To solve this, the authors designed multi-horizon multimodal prediction: supervising the visual latent at a larger future offset (aligned with the executed action horizon) while predicting the tactile latent at the immediate next frame. Combined with a Flow Matching process that generates targets directly from visual-tactile latents without cross-attention layers, they created the ultra-lightweight Agile-WAM architecture.

sections.heading: At the intersection of tactile learning, world models, and Flow Matching
sections.summary: Tactile sensing in robotics has traditionally been used as an extra policy input or for reactive feedback, but is now expanding into world models. Departing from the trend of using massive video foundation models, this paper charts an agile path combining direct Flow Matching with multimodal future prediction.
sections.details:
This work intersects three main research areas:

- Tactile Integration in Robot Learning: Contact forces and slip signals from tactile sensors are critical for manipulation policies. Most prior work, however, merely treats tactile data as an auxiliary observation input to the policy or uses it for reflexive feedback loops. Agile-WAM explicitly includes tactile future prediction in its learning objective, forcing the model to actively internalize contact dynamics.
- World Action Models for Robotics: WAMs equip policies with forward-looking physical understanding by jointly modeling future observations and actions. While visual WAMs are increasingly extended to touch (e.g., Tactile-WAM), existing methods primarily fine-tune large pretrained generative backbones, suffering from heavy inference latency. Agile-WAM replaces these with a lightweight backbone trained from scratch.
- Action Generation via Flow Matching: Compared to diffusion models that iteratively denoise from Gaussian noise, Flow Matching can generate high-quality continuous action trajectories in far fewer integration steps. In particular, methods that use observation latents as the source distribution to construct straight vector fields toward the target (such as VITA) eliminate the need for cross-attention conditioning within the ODE loop. Agile-WAM expands this concept, jointly generating action chunks and future visual/tactile latents in a single unified flow.

sections.heading: How Agile-WAM works: direct Flow Matching and multi-horizon prediction
sections.summary: Current visual, tactile, and proprioceptive observations are encoded into a single shared latent representation. Flow Matching then jointly generates an action chunk and future visual/tactile latents. Key components include a multi-horizon design—predicting a chunk-length horizon for vision and the immediate next frame for touch—and backpropagating prediction errors directly in latent space.
sections.details:
Agile-WAM features a streamlined, efficient pipeline.

### III-A Joint Modeling from Observations to Actions and Future Predictions
At environment step $t$, the robot observes an image $O_t^{\mathrm{vis}}$, tactile signals $O_t^{\mathrm{tac}}$, and joint states $q_t$. The policy $\pi$ jointly generates an action chunk $a_{t:t+H}$ of length $H$ and future observation latents $z_t^{\mathrm{future}} = [z_{t+h_{\mathrm{vis}}}^{\mathrm{vis}}, z_{t+h_{\mathrm{tac}}}^{\mathrm{tac}}]$.

Standard flow-based generation initializes from Gaussian noise and injects observations at every step. Agile-WAM instead treats the shared latent representation of current observations, $z_0$, directly as the source distribution. The target distribution $z_1 = [z_1^a, z_1^{\mathrm{vis}}, z_1^{\mathrm{tac}}]$ concatenates the action and future latents. Along linear interpolation paths across flow time $\tau \in [0,1]$, a lightweight MLP vector field $v_\theta$ learns the velocity field $z_1 - z_0$. Because no additional conditioning is injected during generation, solving the Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) is extremely fast.

### III-B Model Architecture and Training Objectives
The visual encoder is a pretrained ResNet-18, while the tactile encoder is a ResNet-18 trained from scratch to accommodate the spatial structure of TacFF signals. Together with proprioception, these are linearly projected into $z_0$.

To prevent the action space from collapsing, an action autoencoder consisting of encoder $E_a$ and decoder $D_a$ is employed. During training, in addition to the ground-truth action reconstruction loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AE}}$, an action execution loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{act}}$ is computed by decoding the predicted latent $\hat{z}_1^a$ obtained from solving the ODE. Backpropagating this error pulls the generated latents through the ODE integration process directly toward valid, executable actions.

### III-C Multi-Horizon Multimodal Prediction
This is the core insight of the framework. The future tactile latent target is set to the immediate next frame ($h_{\mathrm{tac}} = 1$), while the future visual latent target is set to the execution horizon offset ($h_{\mathrm{vis}} = h = 8$). Because pixel-level video reconstruction is computationally expensive, mean squared error losses $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{vis}}$ and $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{tac}}$ are calculated directly in the encoder latent space. The entire model is optimized end-to-end using a weighted sum of five loss terms, including the Flow Matching loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}$.

sections.heading: 29.4% higher success rate on real-world insertions with 11.9 ms latency
sections.summary: Evaluated across 9 simulation tasks and 5 real-world manipulation tasks, Agile-WAM surpassed state-of-the-art diffusion and flow-based baselines. When misaligned, the robot autonomously executed tactile-guided exploratory search to recover and succeed. A single inference took only 11.9 ms, confirming true real-time performance for high-frequency control.
sections.details:
### IV-A Experimental Setup
The framework was evaluated on 9 tasks in the ManiFeel simulator and 5 real-world tasks using a Flexiv Rizon 4 robot arm: gear assembly, peg insertion, Ethernet cable insertion, Ethernet cable unplugging, and power plug insertion. The robot wrist was equipped with a $32 \times 32$ piezoresistive tactile array and an Intel RealSense D405 camera. Baselines included vision-only Diffusion Policy (DP) and VITA, vision+tactile DP-VT and VITA-VT, and Tactile-WAM (TAAM). Hyperparameters were set to an action chunk size of $H=16$, execution horizon $h=8$, and an Euler solver running for just 6 steps.

### IV-B Performance and Emergent Recovery Behaviors
In real-world experiments, Agile-WAM achieved a 29.4% relative improvement in overall success rate compared to the strongest baseline. It demonstrated remarkable robustness when the in-hand camera was occluded by the target object. In peg insertion, when the peg hit the rim of the hole, vision-only VITA froze, while VITA-VT simply jammed the peg downward and failed. Agile-WAM, in contrast, slid gently across the surface, sensed the rim, located the opening, and completed insertion smoothly. In gear assembly, it detected tooth jamming and made slight rotational wrist adjustments to align the teeth.

### Inference Efficiency
Benchmarked on an RTX 4090, Agile-WAM had an inference latency of just 11.9 ms. This is roughly 40 times faster than DP (487.6 ms with 100 denoising steps), and incurs virtually negligible overhead compared to baseline VITA without future prediction heads (10.7 ms). The additional dimensions in the latent space are easily absorbed by GPU parallelism.

### IV-C & IV-D Ablation Studies
Removing future prediction losses resulted in noticeable performance drops, confirming that gains stem from world model dynamics learning rather than increased parameter capacity. The best performance occurred when observation inputs and prediction targets were multimodal (both vision and touch). In horizon ablations, setting both horizons to +1 degraded vision learning because transitions were trivial, while setting both to +8 caused tactile accuracy to drop due to missed abrupt contact transitions. The combination of +8 for vision and +1 for touch yielded the highest success rates.

sections.heading: Takeaways and future directions
sections.summary: This work proves that an accurate, fast World Action Model can be built by leveraging multi-horizon prediction matched to visual and tactile timescales alongside lightweight Flow Matching. It establishes a practical design paradigm for tactile WAMs capable of high-frequency physical robot manipulation without massive foundation models.
sections.details:
This paper introduced Agile-WAM, an agile tactile World Action Model designed for contact-rich robot control. By directly mapping multimodal observation latents to future states and actions via Flow Matching, the architecture avoids cross-attention and delivers exceptional computational efficiency.

Furthermore, the multi-horizon multimodal prediction scheme—tracking macroscopic scene changes via vision and microscopic contact transitions via touch—plays a decisive role in acquiring delicate, contact-guided recovery skills. Outperforming state-of-the-art baselines in both simulation and real-world experiments while maintaining an ultra-low latency of 11.9 ms, Agile-WAM sets a compelling benchmark for real-time world model deployment in robotics.

takeaways: When training multimodal policies on vision and touch, separating prediction horizons to reflect their different timescales (slower for vision, abrupt for touch) is remarkably effective.
Powerful World Action Models can be trained from scratch using direct Flow Matching without requiring fine-tuning of massive video foundation models.
Setting observation latents directly as the flow source (Direct Flow Matching) removes cross-attention from the generation loop, drastically reducing inference latency on physical robots.
limitations: The method assumes spatial tactile sensors like TacFF or pressure sensor grids, and has not been tested on other modalities such as standard 1-axis or 6-axis force-torque sensors.
Real-world demonstration collection relies on human teleoperation, requiring operators to intentionally include failure and recovery trajectories to teach corrective behaviors.
While policy inference takes only 11.9 ms, overall real-world control frequency is ultimately constrained by sensor hardware sampling rates (30 Hz in these experiments).
